title: Every cellar door in Rutherglen, and what each one actually offers
intro: Rutherglen has more cellar doors per head than anywhere else in the country and almost every guide to it names the same four. This is all of them, with the part nobody prints: what a tasting costs, whether you can walk in, which days they are shut, and whether there is food. Compiled from what each winery publishes itself and last checked on the date below. We have not been to all of them and this is not a ranking. Order runs roughly from the Murray Valley Highway west of town, through the historic estates, and back to Main Street.
author: The LocalsKnow desk

items.blurb: Five generations of the one family, and the tasting happens down among the giant casks rather than across a counter. Back vintage releases are available if you ask. Vineyard platters every day, and groups of ten or more should book.

The refurbished cellar door at Browns Plains pours the fortifieds and the single malt whisky those same barrels went on to shape, which is a genuinely unusual thing to taste side by side. Ten to four, seven days. Tours book separately.
Vines over 120 years old and the wine made on site. Seated tastings ten to four, sales from nine. Closed Sundays unless you arrange it first, which catches people out.

Seated tastings on Jacks Road with a $10 fee refunded against a purchase. Open every day except Christmas. Eight or more, call ahead. About forty five minutes from Albury airport if you are flying in.

Small, personal and two kilometres south of town. Forty five minute tastings at $15 a head, capped at eight, walk ins welcome. Bring your own picnic or pre-order a platter. Dogs on leads are fine and there is a Tesla charger and a bike pump, which tells you who is stopping here.

The most to do at one stop: cellar door and distillery door, seven days, ten to five. The Muscat Mile fortified flight is $15, the guided Barrel Perfection tour with barrel tasting is $35 and needs booking, and the gin tasting is $25. Restaurant on site, bookings essential.

Tasting happens in a heritage listed sales room of handmade brick with the original bark lined roof. Old vine Shiraz, Fiano, Marsanne, Durif and Malbec alongside the fortifieds. Cellar door Wednesday to Sunday, restaurant for lunch Thursday to Sunday.

Estate grown and handmade, on the Chiltern road. Monday to Saturday ten to four, closed Sundays except most long weekends. The museum vault holds back vintages. Walk ins fine, groups appreciated if you book.

Right on the highway between Rutherglen and Yarrawonga, so it is the easy one to fold into a drive. Seven days, ten to five. Standard tastings are free, guided group tastings $10 a head with something to eat alongside. Private tastings need a day's notice.

Vines on the site since 1886 and the first carbon neutral wine business in north east Victoria. Heritage cellar door, a lakeside restaurant, a daily happy hour, and accommodation if you would rather not drive. Sits on the Rutherglen Loops cycle path with bike parking.

In the Tuileries complex on Drummond Street, in cellars Seppelt built in 1886. Italian and Mediterranean varietals rather than the regional standards, tastings bookable online, and a restaurant, courtyard and art gallery in the same complex. The one to pick if the group is split.

Family owned, in 1886 cellars on the highway. Everything made on site from estate grown, non irrigated fruit, and the tasting is with the winemaker rather than a host. Grazing platters at the original homestead. Seven days.

In town on Main Street, working with cool climate fruit rather than Rutherglen's own. Seated tastings with the winemaker, bookings preferred, wine by the glass if you just want a sit down. Garden seating with misting fans, which matters here in February. Closed Tuesday and Wednesday.

title: Eating on Dean Street, Albury, end to end
intro: Dean Street runs about a kilometre from the railway station down to Monument Hill and most of Albury's eating is on it or a few doors off it. This walks the strip in street number order rather than ranking it, because what you actually want to know at seven on a Friday is what is near you and whether it is open. Compiled from what each venue publishes and last checked on the date below. Numbers in brackets are street numbers so you can find them on the map.
author: The LocalsKnow desk

items.blurb: 437, at the station end. North Indian, and one of two Indian kitchens within a hundred metres of each other on this block.
437 as well, in the same building. The long standing Chinese option in the CBD.
443. Mexican, part of a Victorian group that has been going since the seventies, and the reliable one when you are feeding a mixed table.
449A. Small Vietnamese kitchen, and the second of the two Vietnamese options in town.
472. Pizza, on the block where the street starts to fill up in the evening.
479A. Pizza and pasta, near enough to Downtown that the choice is about which room you prefer.
480. Pub, and the one most people mean when they say they will meet you on Dean Street.
484. Daytime, so this is a breakfast and lunch stop rather than a dinner one.
491. Pub with a kitchen, on the corner block.
492, upstairs. Wine bar, which is a different evening to everything else on this list and the reason to look up rather than along.
498. Mediterranean, in the middle of the strip.
546. Toward the top end, past the QEII Square crossing.
593. Pub, at the point where the strip starts to thin out.
610. Thai, and the first of two on the upper blocks.
618. Licensed club rather than a restaurant, with several rooms in it. Worth knowing about when everything else is booked out.
652. The second Thai kitchen, at the Monument Hill end.
662. Indian, right at the top of the street.
664. Breakfast at the very top of Dean Street, which makes it the far end of this walk or the start of it depending on the hour.

title: Beechworth on foot, in one afternoon
intro: Beechworth is compact enough that the whole thing is one walk, and almost all of it is on Ford Street and Camp Street. This is the loop in the order you would actually do it, starting at the historic precinct and ending somewhere with a drink. Forty minutes from Wodonga, an hour from Albury. Compiled from what each place publishes and last checked on the date below.
author: The LocalsKnow desk

items.blurb: 101 Ford Street. Start here. The precinct is the reason the town looks the way it does, and doing it first makes sense of every honey coloured granite building you walk past afterwards.
27 Camp Street. The original one. It is the busiest building in town and that is the point of stopping, not a reason to skip it.
6 Boiler House Lane. Off the main drag, which is exactly why it is the better coffee stop of the two.
52 Ford Street. Italian, mid strip. The lunch option if the bakery queue has put you off.
50 Ford Street. The corner pub, and the landmark everyone navigates by.
42 Ford Street. In the old coach house behind Tanswell's. This is where the walk usually stops, and there is a reason it is hard to leave.
29 Last Street. The other brewery, a block off Ford Street, for anyone who wants to make a comparison of it.
86 Ford Street. Dinner, in an 1856 bank building. Book it before you leave home rather than after the third beer.
44 Ford Street. Cellar door in town, so you can taste Beechworth fruit without driving out to the vineyards.
McConville Avenue. Ten minutes from Ford Street on foot and the easiest way to walk off the afternoon. Free.
McFeeters Road. Five minutes out of town by car rather than on foot, but it is the thing people regret missing. Free.
